ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Approximately 800 participants through subject pools at 4 universities from 4 cultural contexts (one university in Hong Kong China, one university in Canada, one university in India, one university in United Kingdom) were first recruited based on convenience sampling.

> The mean age of participants included was 21.25, with a standard deviation of 4.65.70.40% of participants are women whereas 27.26% of participants are men.

> 0.62% of participants are transgender, 1.09% of participants prefer not to disclose their gender, and 0.62% of participants prefer not to specify their gender.

> Participants completed four questions regarding perceived likelihood (any integer from 0% to 100%) of digital and face-to-face psychological interventions.

> Across all four regions, participants had a higher perceived likelihood of being found out and perceived severity of face loss through face-to-face intervention compared to digital intervention, as shown in Table 3.

> As undergraduate students, participants are likely aware of, and concerned about, the chances of being found out by others (e.g., professors, classmates, or friends) when walking to the university counseling or therapy center, especially at universities where the location of the therapy center is widely known.

> Our results also showed a significantly higher perceived severity of face loss if others found out that participants were undergoing face-to-face intervention.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

live_data_statements: Approximately 800 participants through subject pools at 4 universities from 4 cultural contexts (one university in Hong Kong China, one university in Canada, one university in India, one university in United Kingdom) were first recruited based on convenience sampling.
The mean age of participants included was 21.25, with a standard deviation of 4.65.70.40% of participants are women whereas 27.26% of participants are men.
0.62% of participants are transgender, 1.09% of participants prefer not to disclose their gender, and 0.62% of participants prefer not to specify their gender.
Participants completed four questions regarding perceived likelihood (any integer from 0% to 100%) of digital and face-to-face psychological interventions.

Across all four regions, participants had a higher perceived likelihood of being found out and perceived severity of face loss through face-to-face intervention compared to digital intervention, as shown in Table 3.

As undergraduate students, participants are likely aware of, and concerned about, the chances of being found out by others (e.g., professors, classmates, or friends) when walking to the university counseling or therapy center, especially at universities where the location of the therapy center is widely known.
Our results also showed a significantly higher perceived severity of face loss if others found out that participants were undergoing face-to-face intervention.

text.text: Recent studies have investigated preferences and perceptions towards face-to-face and digital psychological interventions.
Understanding the potential differences in perceived risks between face-to-face and digital services as well as associations with preferences and intentions, can be worthwhile.
We investigated differences in perceived likelihood of being found out and perceived severity of face loss between face-to-face psychological interventions and digital psychological interventions.

We also tested the associations between differences in perceived risks and differences in intentions or preferences towards different types of interventions, and investigated the potential moderation of self-construal, regulatory focus, and cultural background.
We conducted a multi-regional study with 645 college students in Hong Kong China, India, United Kingdom, and Canada.
We performed t-tests, correlation analyses, and moderated multiple regressions, while combining with alternative statistical methods to examine robustness and consistency of findings across methods.

We found that people generally perceive face-to-face interventions to have higher likelihood of being found out and severity of face loss compared to digital interventions, with medium to large effects.

While no significant association was found for the difference in perceived likelihood of being found out with the difference in intervention preferences and help-seeking intentions, higher perceived severity of face loss for face-to-face intervention was associated with lower preferences and intentions for face-to-face intervention relative to digital interventions.

Such associations are moderated by self-construal but in the opposite direction to our hypotheses, in which people with stronger independent self-construal had stronger negative associations between difference in perceived severity of face loss and difference in preferences or intentions.
Our findings contribute by identifying differences in perceived risks between face-to-face and digital interventions as well as association with preferences and intentions.

We speculate the surprising self-construal moderation findings may be due to higher reliance on personal feelings and higher prioritization for self-consistency among more independent people, and call for further studies testing such mechanisms.

We encourage further much-needed investigations into various forms of perceived risks and potential associations with face-to-face or digital mental health intervention preferences, intentions, and decisions, while examining individual and cultural factors.

While face-to-face interventions have long been the primary mode of delivering therapies for people with depression, digital psychological interventions have been shown to be effective for people with depression and have proliferated in the recent decade [1].

text.text: Although some studies with Western samples have found that a higher proportion of people prefer face-to-face over digital interventions [15] [16] [17] [18] [19], people generally perceive greater helpseeking stigma toward face-to-face interventions than toward digital interventions [20].
text.formatted: Although some studies with Western samples have found that a higher proportion of people prefer face-to-face over digital interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>, people generally perceive greater helpseeking stigma toward face-to-face interventions than toward digital interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Although most people generally prefer face-to-face interventions to digital interventions, younger individuals, people with higher attachment avoidance, and people with higher levels of education tend to hold more positive attitudes toward digital interventions [12, 15, 16, 21].

text.text: In particular, individuals who perceive digital interventions as accessible and convenient are more likely to endorse them [22].
text.formatted: In particular, individuals who perceive digital interventions as accessible and convenient are more likely to endorse them <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: Help-seeking preferences and perceptions may also differ across cultures.

In many parts of Asia, access to face-to-face interventions is highly limited because the number of qualified mental health service providers is disproportionately small relative to the overall population [23, 24].
text.formatted: In many parts of Asia, access to face-to-face interventions is highly limited because the number of qualified mental health service providers is disproportionately small relative to the overall population <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24]</ref>.

text.text: Digital psychological interventions, which are generally more accessible, may therefore help address this issue.
In addition, help-seeking stigma has been found to be significantly higher in Asian cultures than in Western cultures [25] [26] [27] [28].
text.formatted: In addition, help-seeking stigma has been found to be significantly higher in Asian cultures than in Western cultures <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, Asian individuals may have greater concerns about face loss, as seeking help for depression may reflect negatively not only on themselves but also on their families and close ones [25] [26] [27] [28].
text.formatted: Specifically, Asian individuals may have greater concerns about face loss, as seeking help for depression may reflect negatively not only on themselves but also on their families and close ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: Given these cultural differences, it may be important to investigate how the perceived risks of being found out and of face loss may affect individuals' preferences for face-to-face versus digital interventions and their intentions to seek these interventions, and to explore potential cultural differences.
Risk perception is multidimensional and among which it can be operationalized along perceived probability and perceived severity [29, 30].
text.formatted: Risk perception is multidimensional and among which it can be operationalized along perceived probability and perceived severity <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30]</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, we examine the perceived probability of being found out and the perceived severity of face loss, as perceived probability and perceived severity are potentially critical factors underlying people's preferences, judgments, and choices [31] [32] [33].
text.formatted: In the present study, we examine the perceived probability of being found out and the perceived severity of face loss, as perceived probability and perceived severity are potentially critical factors underlying people's preferences, judgments, and choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: In general, when perceived risks (probability and/or severity) are high, people may adopt risk-reduction or avoidance strategies by choosing the option with lower perceived risk [34] [35] [36].
text.formatted: In general, when perceived risks (probability and/or severity) are high, people may adopt risk-reduction or avoidance strategies by choosing the option with lower perceived risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref>.

text.text: For perceived severity, we focus specifically on the severity of face loss if one is found out.

Perceived severity of face loss can be defined as the subjective magnitude of negative consequences to the social reputation, social image, and social worth that an individual hopes to maintain [37] [38] [39] [40] [41] [42].
text.formatted: Perceived severity of face loss can be defined as the subjective magnitude of negative consequences to the social reputation, social image, and social worth that an individual hopes to maintain <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref>.

text.text: This construct is particularly relevant because face loss concerns may predict less favorable attitudes toward mental health help-seeking and less help-seeking behavior [37, 43, 44].
text.formatted: This construct is particularly relevant because face loss concerns may predict less favorable attitudes toward mental health help-seeking and less help-seeking behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44]</ref>.

text.text: Many studies worldwide have shown that both mental illness stigma and help-seeking stigma can deter people with mental health challenges from seeking help [6, [45] [46] [47] [48].
text.formatted: Many studies worldwide have shown that both mental illness stigma and help-seeking stigma can deter people with mental health challenges from seeking help <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[45]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[47]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[48]</ref>.

text.text: In cultures where more people hold interdependent self-construals or are more concerned about face, these stigmas are particularly likely to threaten not only one's self-image but also the social reputation of one's close associates, especially family members [25, 42, [49] [50] [51].
text.formatted: In cultures where more people hold interdependent self-construals or are more concerned about face, these stigmas are particularly likely to threaten not only one's self-image but also the social reputation of one's close associates, especially family members <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[49]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[50]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[51]</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, when seeking help for mental health challenges, many people may be likely to worry about the risks of being "found out" and to consider how severe the reputational consequences could be (e.g., face loss for themselves and their families).

These individuals may consider and estimate these risks (likelihood and severity) when making preference judgments and forming intentions regarding the use of face-to-face versus digital psychological interventions.

Because digital psychological interventions, especially those that are self-guided, can be accessed privately in a location that individuals consider safe, many people may perceive them as carrying lower risks of being found out than face-to-face psychological interventions, which must be accessed in person in locations where other people may be present.

Previous studies have found that perceived stigma toward people who seek help through face-to-face interventions is higher than toward those who seek help through digital interventions [20], and that perceived stigma is associated with loss of face [39].
text.formatted: Previous studies have found that perceived stigma toward people who seek help through face-to-face interventions is higher than toward those who seek help through digital interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>, and that perceived stigma is associated with loss of face <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, we hypothesized that people may perceive more serious consequences if family members or others find out about their use of faceto-face interventions than about their use of digital interventions.

Given that some studies have found loss of face concerns to be associated with reduced help-seeking [37, 43] (but see [52] for findings in the opposite direction), it is reasonable to conjecture that people may perceive lower risks for digital interventions than for face-to-face interventions.
text.formatted: Given that some studies have found loss of face concerns to be associated with reduced help-seeking <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43]</ref> (but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[52]</ref> for findings in the opposite direction), it is reasonable to conjecture that people may perceive lower risks for digital interventions than for face-to-face interventions.

text.text: Furthermore, perceived risks have been found to be associated with lower preferences and behavioral intentions to seek help [53].
text.formatted: Furthermore, perceived risks have been found to be associated with lower preferences and behavioral intentions to seek help <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[53]</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, we expected a negative association between relative risk perception (in probability and severity) and relative preferences and intentions in seeking digital and face-toface interventions.

As mentioned, earlier studies, mostly with Western samples, found higher preferences for face-to-face interventions relative to digital interventions, and this may be due to higher perceived effectiveness of face-to-face interventions over digital interventions [15, 18, 19].
text.formatted: As mentioned, earlier studies, mostly with Western samples, found higher preferences for face-to-face interventions relative to digital interventions, and this may be due to higher perceived effectiveness of face-to-face interventions over digital interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, people's preferences for and intentions in seeking face-to-face or digital interventions may be compounded by other factors.
Moreover, the associations between risk perception and preferences may also be moderated by individual and cultural differences, such as regulatory focus and self-construal.

According to Higgins's Regulatory Focus Theory [54], humans have two types of regulatory focus -prevention focus, which concerns safety and security, and promotion focus, which refers to striving for advancements and growth.
text.formatted: According to Higgins's Regulatory Focus Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref>, humans have two types of regulatory focus -prevention focus, which concerns safety and security, and promotion focus, which refers to striving for advancements and growth.

text.text: People with a predominant prevention focus are more concerned about safety when making decisions and more vigilant about potential dangers in their judgments and behaviors [55].
text.formatted: People with a predominant prevention focus are more concerned about safety when making decisions and more vigilant about potential dangers in their judgments and behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref>.

text.text: Building on findings linking prevention focus to lower risk tolerance [56, 57], we speculated that people with a predominant prevention focus may be less willing to tolerate the higher perceived risks of face-to-face interventions.
text.formatted: Building on findings linking prevention focus to lower risk tolerance <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">57]</ref>, we speculated that people with a predominant prevention focus may be less willing to tolerate the higher perceived risks of face-to-face interventions.

text.text: Specifically, we hypothesized that the negative associations between perceived risk of, and preference for, faceto-face interventions over digital interventions would be stronger among people who are predominantly prevention-focused.

In contrast, the associations between differences in perceived risk and differences in preference may be weaker or minimal among people with a predominant promotion focus, as they generally focus more on potential gains and may tolerate higher perceived risks when making judgments and choices [56].
text.formatted: In contrast, the associations between differences in perceived risk and differences in preference may be weaker or minimal among people with a predominant promotion focus, as they generally focus more on potential gains and may tolerate higher perceived risks when making judgments and choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref>.

text.text: Previous studies have shown that people in Asian societies tend to be more prevention-focused, whereas people in Western Europe and North America tend to be more promotion focused [58, 59].
text.formatted: Previous studies have shown that people in Asian societies tend to be more prevention-focused, whereas people in Western Europe and North America tend to be more promotion focused <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[58,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59]</ref>.

text.text: This difference may reflect the more collectivistic cultures in Asia, where people emphasize responsibilities and obligations and may favor prevention-oriented goals, compared with the more individualistic cultures in the West, where people strive for individual aspirations and growth and may favor promotion-oriented goals [58, 59].
text.formatted: This difference may reflect the more collectivistic cultures in Asia, where people emphasize responsibilities and obligations and may favor prevention-oriented goals, compared with the more individualistic cultures in the West, where people strive for individual aspirations and growth and may favor promotion-oriented goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[58,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59]</ref>.

text.text: Given this cultural difference, we hypothesized that the association between differences in perceived risks and differences in preferences or intentions for face-to-face versus digital interventions may be stronger among people in Hong Kong and India than among those in Canada and the United Kingdom.
In addition to regulatory focus, we also examine the potential moderating effects of interdependent and independent self-construal across the four cultures in the present study [60].
text.formatted: In addition to regulatory focus, we also examine the potential moderating effects of interdependent and independent self-construal across the four cultures in the present study <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[60]</ref>.

text.text: Self-construal can be defined as the constellation of feelings, thoughts, and behaviors regarding how people understand the self in relation to others [60] [61] [62].
text.formatted: Self-construal can be defined as the constellation of feelings, thoughts, and behaviors regarding how people understand the self in relation to others <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[60]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">[61]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">[62]</ref>.

text.text: People with higher independent selfconstrual are more focused on demonstrating uniqueness and individuality in their thoughts, traits, goals, and actions, whereas people with higher interdependent self-construal have a self that varies more across contexts and are more concerned about relationships, status, roles, and the "appropriateness" of behaviors [60].
text.formatted: People with higher independent selfconstrual are more focused on demonstrating uniqueness and individuality in their thoughts, traits, goals, and actions, whereas people with higher interdependent self-construal have a self that varies more across contexts and are more concerned about relationships, status, roles, and the "appropriateness" of behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[60]</ref>.

text.text: People with higher interdependent self-construal are more concerned about face when making mental health-related decisions such as help-seeking [25, 50].
text.formatted: People with higher interdependent self-construal are more concerned about face when making mental health-related decisions such as help-seeking <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">50]</ref>.

text.text: Because these individuals consider face more important, we speculate that among more interdependent people, higher perceived risks of being found out and losing face when using face-to-face interventions are more likely to translate into lower preferences for, and intentions to seek, face-to-face interventions relative to digital interventions.

In contrast, among more independent people, the perceived risk of being found out and the perceived severity of losing face when using face-to-face interventions may be less likely to deter them from seeking such help, as they care less about face and more about autonomy in decision-making [63].
text.formatted: In contrast, among more independent people, the perceived risk of being found out and the perceived severity of losing face when using face-to-face interventions may be less likely to deter them from seeking such help, as they care less about face and more about autonomy in decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">[63]</ref>.

text.text: At the cultural level, past studies have shown that people in Asia are, on average, more interdependent, whereas people in the West are, on average, more independent [60, 64, 65].
text.formatted: At the cultural level, past studies have shown that people in Asia are, on average, more interdependent, whereas people in the West are, on average, more independent <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[60,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">64,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">65]</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, it would be reasonable to expect stronger associations between risk perception and preferences or intentions among participants in Hong Kong and India, and weaker associations among participants in Canada and the United Kingdom.

However, given cultural changes in selfconstrual, including increasing individualism and independence in some regions [66, 67], and mixed findings on cross-cultural differences in self-construal (see [68] meta-analysis), we do not rule out the possibility that cultural differences in self-construal may be minimal and that culture may not moderate the association between risk perception and preferences or intentions.

text.text: Approximately 800 participants through subject pools at 4 universities from 4 cultural contexts (one university in Hong Kong China, one university in Canada, one university in India, one university in United Kingdom) were first recruited based on convenience sampling.
Six-hundred and forty-five participants passed our validation checks and are included in analyses.
The validation check consists of five simple questions.
A sample item is "please indicate strongly disagree for this question".
The responses were counted as valid when participants correctly answered all five validation questions.
The mean age of participants included was 21.25, with a standard deviation of 4.65.70.40% of participants are women whereas 27.26% of participants are men.
0.62% of participants are transgender, 1.09% of participants prefer not to disclose their gender, and 0.62% of participants prefer not to specify their gender.
Participants completed four questions regarding perceived likelihood (any integer from 0% to 100%) of digital and face-to-face psychological interventions.

These items included perceived likelihood of being found out by family members through undergoing face-to-face intervention, which is compared with perceived likelihood of being found out by family members through undergoing digital self-guided psychological intervention.

We also included perceived likelihood of being found out by other people (not family members) through undergoing face-to-face intervention, which is compared with perceived likelihood of being found out by other people through undergoing digital self-guided psychological intervention.
Then they completed 6 questions regarding perceived severity of face loss with 0-10 point Likert scales (0 = not at all,10 = very serious).

The first 3 questions in the following are averaged as composite values for perceived severity for face-to-face interventions (α = 0.86) whereas the last 3 questions in the following are averaged as composite for perceived severity of digital interventions (α = 0.86): 1) Perceived severity of personal face loss if family members find out the involvement in face-to-face psychological intervention.
2) Perceived severity of personal face loss if other people find out the involvement in faceto-face psychological intervention.
3) Perceived severity of family face loss if other people find out the involvement in face-toface psychological intervention.
4) Perceived severity of personal face loss if family members find out the involvement in digital psychological intervention.
5) Perceived severity of personal face loss if other people find out the involvement in digital psychological intervention.
6) Perceived severity of family face loss if other people find out the involvement in digital psychological intervention.

The survey also consists of one question on the extent they prefer face-to-face intervention and another preference question for digital intervention, with 0 to 10 Likert scales (0 = Not at all,10 = Highly prefer).

A difference in preference score for face-to-face intervention versus digital intervention is calculated (preference of face-to-face intervention -preference of digital intervention), in which a positive score implies stronger preference for face-to-face intervention and a negative score implies stronger preference for digital intervention.
Similar scoring approaches have been adopted in health preference studies [77].

text.text: They also completed 3 questions (1 = Strongly disagree,6 = Strongly agree) on intentions of seeking help through face-to-face intervention (α = 0.91) and 3 questions for digital intervention (α = 0.95).

Similar to preference, a difference in intention score is computed (behavioral intention for face-to-face intervention -behavioral intention for digital intervention), with a positive score implying stronger intention for face-to-face intervention and a negative score implying stronger intention for digital intervention.
The survey also consists of individual difference scales on regulatory focus and self-construal.
The survey consists of the 11-item Regulatory Focus Questionnaire by Higgins et al. [78], which measures participants' motivational orientations (prevention focus versus promotion focus).

text.text: To summarize, we found no support for the hypothesized cultural moderation effect and cultural differences in self-construal, and weak evidence for differences in regulatory focus.
We concluded that we found no evidence for the hypothesized indirect moderation.
Our study found support for a substantially higher perceived likelihood of being found out for face-to-face intervention than for digital intervention, with a large effect size.
We also found strong effects with Wilcoxon rank tests, implying that the differences are robust when ranking within-pair differences.
This difference in the perceived likelihood of being found out is understandable, and participants' risk perceptions may, to some extent, reflect actual risks.

As undergraduate students, participants are likely aware of, and concerned about, the chances of being found out by others (e.g., professors, classmates, or friends) when walking to the university counseling or therapy center, especially at universities where the location of the therapy center is widely known.
In contrast, some students can access digital mental health platforms more privately on their smartphones and computers, so the actual or perceived likelihood of being found out is lower.
However, access to private space varies across individuals (see [4] for a review).
text.formatted: However, access to private space varies across individuals (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> for a review).

text.text: Future studies investigating the actual likelihood of being found out among participants who have undergone, or are currently undergoing, digital versus face-to-face interventions would be worthwhile.
Such studies could test whether these differences in perceived risks align with actual risks or reflect overestimations of risk.
In addition, it is uncertain whether these face-to-face versus digital gaps in perceived or actual risks generalize to the working population and older adults.

Most people do not have access to the free face-to-face counseling services available at universities, and the locations of therapy centers are less likely to be known by people who know the potential service users.
Another form of perceived risk is the perceived severity of face loss if others find out.
Our results also showed a significantly higher perceived severity of face loss if others found out that participants were undergoing face-to-face intervention.
These findings are consistent with those of a previous study that found higher perceived stigma for face-to-face intervention than for digital intervention [20].
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with those of a previous study that found higher perceived stigma for face-to-face intervention than for digital intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Perceived severity of face loss (but perhaps not perceived likelihood) appears to be conceptually and empirically associated with perceived stigma [39, 49], as both face loss and stigma concern social image and reputation [37, 51, 97].

text.text: Although we did not investigate the possible mechanisms, the higher perceived severity of face loss for face-to-face intervention may arise because people generally believe that face-to-face interventions are for people with more severe mental illnesses.
In contrast, digital interventions may be perceived as more suitable for people with mild mental health issues or life challenges.
The severity of mental health challenges appears to be associated with the severity of stigma [98].
text.formatted: The severity of mental health challenges appears to be associated with the severity of stigma <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">[98]</ref>.

text.text: We speculate that this partly explains why the perceived severity of face loss, which is positively associated with perceived stigma, is higher for face-to-face intervention.

Furthermore, because our study focused on self-guided digital intervention rather than video psychotherapy or counseling, the perceived severity of face loss for digital intervention may have been lower than it would be for guided intervention.
This is because self-help may be perceived as more acceptable and as carrying relatively lower stigma concerns [99].
text.formatted: This is because self-help may be perceived as more acceptable and as carrying relatively lower stigma concerns <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">[99]</ref>.

text.text: Future studies are needed to test this speculation.

Are relative perceived risks (i.e., the perceived risk of face-to-face interventions minus the perceived risk of digital interventions) associated with preferences and intentions for face-to-face versus digital interventions?
Interestingly, we found a significant association between the perceived severity of face loss if found out and differences in intervention preferences and intentions.
However, we found no significant association between the perceived likelihood of being found out and intervention preferences and intentions.

The significant association of preferences or intentions with the perceived severity of threat (face loss in this context) is consistent with studies on the link between perceived severity and intention or behavior in the broader health behavior literature [33, 100], including the mental health help-seeking literature In contrast to the significant findings with perceived severity as the predictor, the minimal association (rs < 0.03, not significant) between the difference in perceived likelihood and preferences or intentions was unexpected and inconsistent with the broader literature on perceived likelihood and health behavior [102].

text.text: One possible explanation is that "being found out" is not necessarily detrimental to one's intention to seek help, whereas "losing face" is often a negative consequence that people seek to avoid.
Risk of losing face may therefore have more influence on the decision to seek help.
It is possible that some people are not worried about the chances of being found out, perhaps because of lower face concern and more accepting professors, classmates, and friends.
However, this explanation is speculative.
Future studies may conceptually replicate these findings with different samples in different settings and examine potential moderators.
In the previous section, we discussed the association between perceived risk and preferences or intentions in general (i.e., on average).
However, these associations could vary depending on one's cultural characteristics.

Contrary to our hypothesis, which predicted a stronger association between perceived severity and preferences or intentions among more interdependent people, we found that the association between the perceived severity of face loss and intention (and possibly preferences) was stronger among people with higher independent self-construal.

One possible explanation is that people with higher independent self-construal have less need to justify their preferences or choices to others, so they may rely more on personal feelings when forming preference judgments and making choices [103].
text.formatted: One possible explanation is that people with higher independent self-construal have less need to justify their preferences or choices to others, so they may rely more on personal feelings when forming preference judgments and making choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">[103]</ref>.

text.text: Although earlier work tended to theorize risk perception as a purely or predominantly cognitive process [104], some studies in the past two decades have found positive associations between affective feelings and risk perception in some contexts [105, 106].
text.formatted: Although earlier work tended to theorize risk perception as a purely or predominantly cognitive process <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">[104]</ref>, some studies in the past two decades have found positive associations between affective feelings and risk perception in some contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">[105,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">106]</ref>.

text.text: When participants answer questions about the perceived severity of face loss, which may be very emotionally uncomfortable, they may plausibly rely more on their feelings, especially if they are predominantly independent.
Because such risk perception is partly associated with feelings, it may then relate more strongly to preferences and behavioral intentions among independent people [103].
text.formatted: Because such risk perception is partly associated with feelings, it may then relate more strongly to preferences and behavioral intentions among independent people <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">[103]</ref>.

text.text: Our findings are also conceptually consistent with studies showing a stronger association between concern about (or perceived severity of) environmental problems and pro-environmental behavioral intentions or behavior in more individualistic societies [107, 108].
text.formatted: Our findings are also conceptually consistent with studies showing a stronger association between concern about (or perceived severity of) environmental problems and pro-environmental behavioral intentions or behavior in more individualistic societies <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">[107,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">108]</ref>.

text.text: This may be because people with stronger independent self-construal consider personal attributes (including the perceived severity of an issue) more important.
Personal attitudes are also more closely aligned with behavioral intentions or behaviors among people who are more individualistic or have higher independent self-construal [107] [108] [109].
text.formatted: Personal attitudes are also more closely aligned with behavioral intentions or behaviors among people who are more individualistic or have higher independent self-construal <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">[107]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">[108]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">[109]</ref>.

text.text: People with stronger independent selfconstrual prioritize consistency, whereas consistency may matter less to people with lower independent self-construal [110].
text.formatted: People with stronger independent selfconstrual prioritize consistency, whereas consistency may matter less to people with lower independent self-construal <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">[110]</ref>.

text.text: In the context of our study, consider people with stronger independent self-construal who perceive a higher risk of face loss for face-to-face interventions than for digital interventions.
For these people, preferring or intending to engage in digital interventions would be more consistent with their risk perception.

In contrast, among people with lower independent self-construal, the association between the perceived severity of face loss and preferences or behavioral intentions becomes weaker or nonsignificant, possibly because they care much less about consistency.
Our explanations are speculative and require replication or follow-up studies.
Further research can also examine the potential mechanisms, including mediating or moderating variables such as reliance on feelings [103] and self-consistency [110].
text.formatted: Further research can also examine the potential mechanisms, including mediating or moderating variables such as reliance on feelings <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">[103]</ref> and self-consistency <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">[110]</ref>.

text.text: Apart from self-construal, we found no support for the hypothesized moderation of regulatory focus.

We based our hypothesis on research into the association between regulatory focus and risk tolerance in financial and physician decision making [56, 57], but not preferences or behavioral intentions for help-seeking in mental health contexts.
text.formatted: We based our hypothesis on research into the association between regulatory focus and risk tolerance in financial and physician decision making <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">57]</ref>, but not preferences or behavioral intentions for help-seeking in mental health contexts.

text.text: It is also important to recognize that the association between regulatory focus and risk taking is not as straightforward as previously assumed.
Some studies have found that some prevention-focused people may be more willing to take risks when they need to restore the status quo after experiencing financial losses [111, 112].
text.formatted: Some studies have found that some prevention-focused people may be more willing to take risks when they need to restore the status quo after experiencing financial losses <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">[111,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">112]</ref>.

text.text: However, whether such effects are generalizable to mental health intervention contexts is uncertain.

Although self-construal moderated the association, we found no support for a moderating effect of culture (Asian regions: Hong Kong and India; Western regions: Canada and the United Kingdom) on the association between perceived severity and preferences or intentions.
Findings were relatively consistent across regions: all four regions showed significant associations between differences in perceived severity and differences in preferences.
This may be because the differences in self-construal between regions did not even reach significance.
Surprisingly, participants from the United Kingdom and Canada scored higher on interdependent self-construal than on independent self-construal.
This finding was unexpected and contradicts some earlier studies and claims about cultural differences in self-construal and individualism/collectivism [60, 64].
text.formatted: This finding was unexpected and contradicts some earlier studies and claims about cultural differences in self-construal and individualism/collectivism <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[60,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">64]</ref>.

text.text: One explanation may be the particular characteristics of participants at the Canadian and British universities where we collected data.

Another explanation is that cross-cultural differences in self-construal are relatively weak and inconsistent across samples, as shown in Levine et al. 's [68] meta-analysis of cross-cultural selfconstrual research and in more recent studies [113].
text.formatted: Another explanation is that cross-cultural differences in self-construal are relatively weak and inconsistent across samples, as shown in Levine et al. 's <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">[68]</ref> meta-analysis of cross-cultural selfconstrual research and in more recent studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">[113]</ref>.

text.text: We also note that ethnic minorities (non-Caucasian participants, including some Asian and African participants) made up a substantial proportion of our Canadian (30.99%) and British (29.29%) samples.
However, our exploratory analyses (see Supplementary Table S5) found no significant differences in self-construal between Caucasian and Asian participants.
text.formatted: However, our exploratory analyses (see Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">S5</ref>) found no significant differences in self-construal between Caucasian and Asian participants.

text.text: Across different regions, a larger proportion of participants were predominantly preventionfocused and interdependent, yet more than 35% of participants in each region were predominantly promotion-focused and independent (see Supplementary Tables S5 and S6).
text.formatted: Across different regions, a larger proportion of participants were predominantly preventionfocused and interdependent, yet more than 35% of participants in each region were predominantly promotion-focused and independent (see Supplementary Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">S5</ref> and <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">S6</ref>).

text.text: Given this diversity in individual characteristics (e.g., self-construal) within each region, researchers and practitioners may focus more on individual differences than on cultural background.
Individual differences in self-construal appear to play a more meaningful role in explaining the associations between differences in risk perception and differences in preferences or intentions.
One of the strengths of our study is that multi-regional data increases the generalizability of the findings.
Cross-regional studies on digital mental health versus in-person intervention preferences or perceptions are rare.
We encourage more such studies to test whether findings generalize and how they vary across cultures.

Because our findings contradict some crosscultural studies on self-construal, future studies could examine the potential role of culture in the association between perceived risk and preferences or intentions, using more representative or more diverse samples.
Regarding generalizability, because our participants were college students, it is uncertain, and possibly limited, how far our findings extend to the general population.

As discussed earlier, the perceived likelihood of being found out when using face-to-face interventions may be higher in campus settings, because many people who study or work at a university likely know where its counseling or psychotherapy center is located.

Future studies could examine whether, among working adults and older adults, the perceived likelihood of being found out and the perceived severity of face loss differ substantially between face-to-face and digital interventions.
Our work takes a pioneering step by comparing the perceived risks of face-to-face and digital mental health interventions, measuring risk as both likelihood and severity.
However, we did not examine other operationalizations of risk perception.
Studies comparing perceptions of, and preferences for, face-to-face and digital mental health interventions rarely examine risk perception.
In contrast, various operationalizations of risk perception are frequently studied in judgment and decision making, social psychology, and health psychology [106, 114, 115].
text.formatted: In contrast, various operationalizations of risk perception are frequently studied in judgment and decision making, social psychology, and health psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">[106,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">114,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">115]</ref>.

text.text: We hope our study will inspire research on other operationalizations of risk perception (e.g., intuition-based perceived vulnerability and affective risk perception [114]).
text.formatted: We hope our study will inspire research on other operationalizations of risk perception (e.g., intuition-based perceived vulnerability and affective risk perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">[114]</ref>).

text.text: We also hope it will inspire research on the perceived risks of other potential threats associated with engaging in faceto-face versus digital interventions (e.g., professional or occupational risks, risks of adverse effects, and privacy risks).
Such research may help explain individual differences in preferences for, and choices between, digital and face-to-face interventions.
Furthermore, we found that self-construal moderated the association between differences in perceived severity and differences in preferences or intentions.
However, the direction of this effect was opposite to what we expected, and its mechanisms require further investigation.
Such effects may be due to differences in reliance of feelings on behavior and prioritization for selfconsistency between people with different levels of independent self-construal.
Because our study did not measure these variables directly, future studies may try to replicate our findings and examine potential mechanisms.
They may do so by including additional mediating or moderating variables, notably self-consistency [110] and reliance on feelings [103].
text.formatted: They may do so by including additional mediating or moderating variables, notably self-consistency <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">[110]</ref> and reliance on feelings <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">[103]</ref>.

text.text: Pending further research investigations before widespread implementations, our findings may have potential implications for designs of future decision aid for in-person vs digital interventions [14] and mental health practitioners when working with individuals with higher perceived severity of face loss, who had experienced severe face loss, and/or people who are more independent.
text.formatted: Pending further research investigations before widespread implementations, our findings may have potential implications for designs of future decision aid for in-person vs digital interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> and mental health practitioners when working with individuals with higher perceived severity of face loss, who had experienced severe face loss, and/or people who are more independent.

text.text: For these individuals, face loss and the perceived risk of face loss may discourage them from continuing to see a psychotherapist and from disclosing comfortably during therapy sessions.

Psychotherapists and psychotherapy researchers may explore ways to address concerns regarding the negative consequences of face loss and the perceived risk of face loss, for example through strength-based approaches [39].
text.formatted: Psychotherapists and psychotherapy researchers may explore ways to address concerns regarding the negative consequences of face loss and the perceived risk of face loss, for example through strength-based approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref>.

text.text: It is possible that mitigating the experienced and the perceived severity of face loss may result in higher attendances or engagements in psychotherapy, but further research is needed to examine this possibility before applying in the real-world.

In addition, decision aid for face-to-face and/or digital mental health support seeking decisions [14], may consider incorporating face loss concerns, actual, and perceived risks, as potential attributes in the design, going beyond effectiveness and limitations.

text.text: To address the concerns of people who perceive a very high risk of face loss in face-to-face interventions, practitioners, mental health promoters, and researchers may test whether digital mental health platforms are promoted more effectively when messages emphasize that using these platforms in private, personal spaces carries a lower risk of face loss or less concerns of face loss.ConclusionTo conclude, our work contributes to the growing literature of perceptions and preferences for psychological interventions, with novel, strong and cross-regionally generalizable findings of substantially higher perceived risks, in terms of both likelihood and severity, through face-toface psychological interventions compared to digital psychological interventions.

Furthermore, higher perceived severity for face-to-face interventions compared to digital interventions is associated with lower preferences or intentions for face-to-face interventions compared to digital interventions.
Such association is moderated by independent self-construal, with stronger association among more independent individuals.
More studies are needed to investigate the mechanisms of such surprising findings.

Finally, we call for further studies extending on our pioneering study on perceived risks by examining different forms of perceived risks of digital and face-to-face interventions and their associations with preferences, intentions, and decisionmaking of interventions, while considering individual characteristics and cultural factors.
